## Why This Is Asked

Quickly verifies ability to apply a standard trick across a wide-width type and reason about cross-boundary bits.

## Key Concepts

- Bitwise shifts, AND, and masks
- Edge cases at 64-bit boundary
- O(1) implementation without loops

## Code Example

```c
uint128 hasConsecutiveOnes128(uint128 x) {
  return (uint128)((x & (x >> 1)) != 0);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you adapt to return the count of consecutive-ones pairs?
- How would you extend to 256-bit values and vectorized code?

## Why This Question Is Asked
Tests the ability to decompose a 128-bit integer into 32-bit lanes and recombine them in a different order without using branches.

## Key Concepts
- Representing a 128-bit integer as two 64-bit halves (hi and lo)
- Extracting 32-bit lanes using bit masks and shifts
- Reassembling via shifts and bitwise ORs

## Common Pitfalls
- Confusing the mapping between bits and lanes
- Forgetting to mask after right-shifting (to isolate the lower 32 bits)
- Incorrectly pairing the extracted lanes when reassembling

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests the ability to reason about 128-bit bit patterns and leverage existing helper functions to implement non-trivial properties without using conditional branches.

## Key Concepts
- Bit reversal and palindrome detection in 128-bit space
- Constant-time, branchless implementation
- Integration with existing `reverse128` utility

## Code Example
```c
int isPalindrome128(uint64_t hi, uint64_t lo) {
  uint64_t rhi, rlo;
  reverse128(hi, lo, &rhi, &rlo);
  return (rhi == hi && rlo == lo);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you extend this approach to 256-bit values?
- What optimizations could be applied if the function were called frequently?
